metadata.research_goal: Create backend-oriented coaching and rule models for indoor six-player volleyball: rotation state, overlap validation, front-row/back-row legal constraints, libero and substitution handling, and practical 4-2, 6-2, and 5-1 system progressions.

source_refs.title: Official Volleyball Rules 2025-2028
source_refs.notes: Primary international indoor rules text. Key backend references: rally scoring, six-player line-up order, 2025 receiving-team positional constraints, rotation order, service screening, attack-hit limits, block limits, substitution limits, and libero actions.

source_refs.title: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition
source_refs.organization_or_author: FIVB Rules of the Game and Refereeing Commission
source_refs.notes: Official interpretations for the 2025-2028 rule text. Useful for edge-case handling such as screening, back-row setter attack faults, and libero overhand finger-pass restrictions.

source_refs.title: Coaches Manual Level II
source_refs.notes: Defines the common offensive system notation and coaching considerations for 4-2, 5-1, and 6-2 systems, including penetrating vs non-penetrating setters, switching, serve-receive formations, attack balance, and team coordination.

source_refs.title: 2025-2027 USAV Indoor Rules Book
source_refs.notes: United States national rulebook. Important differences from FIVB include 15 substitutions per set in standard USAV play, expanded individual substitute entries, and libero serving in one rotation position.

source_refs.title: Rulebooks and Interpretations
source_refs.notes: Official portal for USAV indoor rulebooks, abridged rulebooks, casebooks, scoring instructions, and interpretation updates. Use as the first update check before building production rule variants.

source_refs.title: Rules of Volleyball
source_refs.notes: Plain-language explanation of 6 vs 6 volleyball, clockwise rotation, front-row/back-row distinction, libero overview, and examples of 5-1 and 6-2 team organization.

source_refs.title: Why Should I Run a 6-3 or 6-6?
source_refs.notes: Development-focused coaching resource. Useful for beginner and youth progression decisions, simplified serve-receive patterns, reduced switching, and delaying early specialization.

source_refs.title: Recipe for a Setter
source_refs.notes: Coaching resource on setter selection and demands. Used for 5-1 implications because a single setter carries repeated second-contact, communication, leadership, and decision-making responsibility.

source_refs.title: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
source_refs.notes: Summarizes common volleyball injury patterns and prevention principles. Relevant to system-driven load management: ankle sprains at the net, patellar tendinopathy from jump volume, shoulder overuse, and low back load.

key_concepts.name: Six-player rally scoring base
key_concepts.definition: Indoor volleyball is modeled as six players per team in play. Every completed rally awards a point; a team winning a rally while receiving gains the next service and must rotate before serving.
key_concepts.backend_use: Anchor match state, score state, set state, and rotation-state transitions.

teaching_implications.beginner: Teach that winning serve receive creates both a point and a clockwise rotation.
teaching_implications.intermediate: Connect rotation order to serve order, substitution legality, and who is front row.
teaching_implications.advanced: Track scoring efficiency by rotation because each rotation changes attacker availability and defensive matchups.

key_concepts.name: Rotation order and court positions
key_concepts.definition: The submitted starting line-up creates a fixed rotational order for the set. Court positions are 4 front-left, 3 front-center, 2 front-right, 5 back-left, 6 back-center, and 1 back-right.
key_concepts.backend_use: Generate legal line-up snapshots, player front/back status, serving order, rotation labels, and role availability.

key_concepts.name: Front-row and back-row status
key_concepts.definition: A player's current rotational position, not their named role, determines whether they are front row or back row for attack and blocking restrictions.
key_concepts.backend_use: Drive legal action checks for attacking, blocking, back-row setter decisions, libero replacement eligibility, and role prompts in drills.

key_concepts.name: Receiving-team overlap model
key_concepts.definition: At service contact, the receiving team must remain in rotational order. Each back-row player must be no closer to the center line than the corresponding front-row player, and each row must preserve left-center-right order by foot position.
key_concepts.backend_use: Validate legal serve-receive formations and generate overlap warnings in rotation diagrams.
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition

teaching_implications.beginner: Use simple pair language: left with left, middle with middle, right with right.
teaching_implications.intermediate: Teach players to identify the two teammates they must stay relative to before the serve.
teaching_implications.advanced: Use legal compression to hide passers, protect weak passers, and release specialized players immediately after service contact.

key_concepts.name: Serving-team position freedom under FIVB 2025-2028
key_concepts.definition: Under the current FIVB text, the receiving team must satisfy rotational order at service contact, while players of the serving team are free to occupy any position at service contact. The serving team still must serve in the correct rotational order and comply with screening rules.
key_concepts.backend_use: Prevent older overlap validators from incorrectly flagging serving-team positions. Separate service-order faults from receiving-team positional faults.
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition

key_concepts.name: Attack-line constraint for back-row attackers
key_concepts.definition: Back-row players may complete an attack hit at any height only when taking off from behind the attack line. If a back-row player attacks from the front zone while the ball is entirely higher than the net, it is an attack fault.
key_concepts.backend_use: Flag illegal back-row attacks, back-row setter dump risks, pipe/bic eligibility, and drill constraints.
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition

key_concepts.name: Block eligibility
key_concepts.definition: Only front-row players may complete a block. Back-row players and liberos may not complete or participate in a completed block; blocking the opponent's service is illegal.
key_concepts.backend_use: Validate block participation and generate role-specific responsibilities in front-row vs back-row rotations.

key_concepts.name: Libero specialist constraints
key_concepts.definition: The libero is a back-row defensive specialist who may replace any back-row player without counting as a regular substitution. A libero cannot block, cannot attempt to block, and under FIVB cannot serve. The libero cannot complete an attack hit when the ball is entirely higher than the net.
key_concepts.backend_use: Model defensive substitutions, libero availability, serve-receive formations, and attack/block action filters.

key_concepts.name: Regular substitution pairing
key_concepts.definition: FIVB allows six regular substitutions per set. A starter may leave and re-enter only once, and only in their original line-up position; a substitute may enter for one starter and be replaced only by that same starter. USAV standard indoor play permits 15 substitutions per set with more flexible repeat entries within the same line-up position.
key_concepts.backend_use: Support rule-set-specific roster state and legal substitution recommendation logic.

key_concepts.name: Completed-rally gate
key_concepts.definition: Several roster actions require a completed rally between repeated requests or replacements: separate regular substitution requests by the same team and most libero replacements.
key_concepts.backend_use: Prevent illegal consecutive substitutions or libero swaps during the same dead-ball interval.

key_concepts.name: Offensive system number notation
key_concepts.definition: Common volleyball system notation describes primary attackers and primary setters. In practical coaching use, 4-2 uses two setters and four hitters, 5-1 uses one setter and five hitters, and 6-2 uses two setters who also attack, with the back-row setter running the offense.
key_concepts.backend_use: Normalize system profiles, teaching progression, and rotation-generated responsibilities.

technical_models.name: Serve-contact overlap validator
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition

inputs.player_positions: array of {player_id, rotation_position, foot_x_lateral, foot_y_depth, last_floor_contact_x, last_floor_contact_y}
inputs.court_orientation: which direction is toward the center line for this team

validation_logic.condition: ruleset starts with FIVB_2025_2028 and team_phase is serving
validation_logic.result: skip positional overlap checks; validate service order and screen separately
check front-back pair depth and same-row lateral order at service contact
release players to any legal playing location; preserve action legality by row status

common_backend_errors_to_avoid: Do not use player role names as row status; a setter can be front row or back row depending on rotation.
Do not validate receiving-team overlap after the serve has been contacted.
Do not apply pre-2025 serving-team overlap checks to FIVB 2025-2028 matches.
Do not use torso position alone; the rules anchor position by the feet contacting the floor or the last floor contact.

state_fields.lineup_order: array of six player ids in rotational order
state_fields.front_row_player_ids: array of player ids in positions 4, 3, 2
state_fields.back_row_player_ids: array of player ids in positions 5, 6, 1

transitions.rotation_effect: receiving team rotates clockwise before serving next
faulting team order rectified; later points may be cancelled if exact fault moment is known

technical_models.name: Legal action matrix by row and role

matrix.notes: Must contact ball within own playing space except normal blocking rules.

matrix.can_attempt_block: attempt without completed block is still high risk for fault if participating in a completed block
matrix.notes: Back-row setter dumps are illegal if the setter takes off in the front zone and the ball is entirely above the net when the completed attack occurs.

matrix.can_serve_usav: yes, in one rotation position after replacing the player in position 1
matrix.notes: The libero is always treated as a back-row player regardless of physical location after the serve.

technical_models.name: Libero replacement state model

state_fields.designated_liberos: array of zero, one, or two player ids

legal_replacement_rules: Libero may replace only a player in a back-row position.
Libero replacement does not count as a regular substitution.
The regular replacement player may replace or be replaced by either libero.
The acting libero may be replaced only by the regular replacement player for that position or by the second libero.
Except for listed rule exceptions, there must be a completed rally between two libero replacements.
Libero replacement occurs while the ball is out of play and before the whistle for service; first late replacement is normally allowed with warning, repeated lateness risks delay sanction.

usav_variant.service_scope: one position in the rotation after replacing the player in position 1
usav_variant.set_to_set_designation_flexibility: USAV permits zero, one, or two liberos for each set with constraints based on match-start designations.

technical_models.name: Regular substitution state model
backend_checks: Track substitutions by set, not match.
Track line-up position, not just player id.
Exclude libero replacements from regular substitution counts.
Reject second separate substitution request in the same interruption unless injury, illness, expulsion, or disqualification exception applies.

technical_models.name: Offensive system profile model
source_refs: Why Should I Run a 6-3 or 6-6?

systems.front_row_attackers_when_setter_back_row: not normally used as a back-row penetrating setter system
systems.teaching_focus: stable target, fewer long setter runs, clear front-row setter identity, rotation understanding
systems.load_implications: lower setter movement load; fewer front-row attack options than 5-1 or 6-2

systems.substitution_dependency: depends_on_roster_and_ruleset; often uses opposite-setter pairs or double substitutions
systems.teaching_focus: back-row setter penetration, three front-row attackers, coordination between two setters, legal back-row setter decisions
systems.load_implications: two setter-attackers share setting but also carry attacking/blocking load when front row

systems.substitution_dependency: low_to_moderate; can use double subs in some rule sets but must manage FIVB six-sub limit
systems.teaching_focus: one offensive decision-maker, consistent tempo, opposite hitter role, rotation-by-rotation side-out planning
systems.load_implications: high cognitive and movement load on one setter; opposite and outside attackers often carry heavy attacking responsibility

tactical_rules.name: Serve-receive overlap before release
tactical_rules.if: team is receiving and referee has authorized service
tactical_rules.then: each player must stay legally ordered by foot position until service contact, then may release to specialized base or attack-preparation locations
coaching_cues: Know the front/back teammate you must stay behind or in front of.
Know the same-row teammate you must stay left or right of.
Release on contact, not on the server's toss.

tactical_rules.name: Serving-team screening constraint
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition
tactical_rules.then: players may position freely under FIVB 2025-2028, but may not prevent the receiver from seeing the service hit and ball path; serving-team players may not raise hands above the head during service until the ball has passed beyond the net
coaching_cues: Use legal defensive base locations without hiding the server or ball path.
Keep hands below head level during service sequence.
Do not let free serving-team positioning become a screen fault.

tactical_rules.name: Back-row setter attack fault guardrail
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition
tactical_rules.if: setter is in a back-row rotational position and jumps in the front zone with ball entirely above the net
tactical_rules.then: do not send the ball across or into an opponent's block; set a teammate or contact below the relevant height threshold
coaching_cues: Back-row setter jump sets are legal when the ball is set to a teammate and does not become an illegal completed attack.
Avoid emergency second-ball pushes over the net from inside the front zone.
Teach setters their rotational row before teaching setter dumps.

tactical_rules.name: Libero front-zone set guardrail
source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition
tactical_rules.if: libero uses an overhand finger pass while in the front zone or its extension
tactical_rules.then: teammates may not complete an attack hit while the ball is entirely higher than the top of the net
coaching_cues: Train liberos to bump-set when inside the front zone if the hitter may contact above the net.
Use overhand libero sets freely from behind the attack line extension.
Teach attackers to recognize when the libero set legally limits above-net attack.

tactical_rules.name: Front-row block responsibility
tactical_rules.then: player is eligible to block and should be assigned block responsibilities appropriate to role and matchup
coaching_cues: Only front-row players can close a legal block.
Back-row players defend behind or around the block.
A libero must not attempt to block.

tactical_rules.name: Rotation release to base
tactical_rules.if: serve has been contacted and team is no longer constrained by overlap
tactical_rules.then: players should move to system base positions that support setter access, attack balance, blocking matchups, and defensive coverage
coaching_cues: Switch after service contact with a defined path.
Minimize switches for beginners; add specialization only when players can move without losing ball focus.
Evaluate whether switching improves attack balance enough to justify transition complexity.

tactical_rules.name: FIVB six-sub strategy
tactical_rules.then: avoid substitution-heavy system choices unless the tactical benefit is worth the limited bench flexibility
coaching_cues: A 6-2 built on frequent setter/opposite exchanges may be constrained by six substitutions.
A 5-1 provides offensive continuity with lower substitution dependency.
Plan injury and late-set serving/defensive substitutions before using double substitutions early.

tactical_rules.name: USAV fifteen-sub strategy
tactical_rules.then: teams can more practically use front-row/back-row specialists, double subs, and setter/opposite exchanges, while still tracking line-up position legality
coaching_cues: Use the extra substitution budget to develop role specialists without breaking line-up position rules.
Do not confuse USAV flexibility with libero replacement rules.
Track substitutions by line-up position and by set.

tactical_rules.name: 4-2 use case
source_refs: Why Should I Run a 6-3 or 6-6?
tactical_rules.if: team is learning six-player volleyball or lacks stable setter penetration
tactical_rules.then: use 4-2 to keep a setter near the net, reduce confusion, and teach rotation structure before specialization

tactical_rules.name: 6-2 use case
tactical_rules.if: team has two setters who can also attack/block and can coordinate back-row setter penetration
tactical_rules.then: use 6-2 to keep three front-row attackers available while the back-row setter runs the offense

advantages: three front-row attackers in every rotation
costs: possible substitution pressure depending on ruleset

tactical_rules.name: 5-1 use case
tactical_rules.if: team has one reliable setter capable of leading all six rotations
tactical_rules.then: use 5-1 for consistent offensive decision-making and tempo, accepting that front-row setter rotations have only two other front-row attackers

costs: large cognitive and movement load on one setter
front-row setter rotations need planned scoring options
setter size/blocking can affect right-front matchups

physical_demands.name: Front-row jump density
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
physical_demands.description: Front-row players carry repeated jump demands for attacking, blocking, block transitions, and coverage. Middle blockers and front-row opposites often have dense repeated-jump sequences because they must read, move laterally, block, land, and transition to attack.
physical_demands.backend_use: Attach jump-volume warnings to front-row-heavy practice plans and position-specific load estimates.
training_considerations: track block jumps and attack jumps separately
avoid excessive jump volume in early technical learning blocks

physical_demands.name: Setter penetration movement load
physical_demands.description: Penetrating systems require a back-row setter to move from a back-row rotational starting point into a setting target while preserving overlap until service contact. This adds sprint, deceleration, orientation, and decision load.
physical_demands.backend_use: Increase movement complexity and cognitive load tags for 5-1 and 6-2 rotation drills.
training_considerations: practice setter release paths by rotation
include emergency setting when pass pulls setter off target
separate no-ball footwork from live serve receive before adding full speed

physical_demands.name: Single-setter cognitive load
physical_demands.description: A 5-1 concentrates offensive communication, tempo management, play calling, and second-contact decision-making in one setter across all six rotations.
physical_demands.backend_use: Tag 5-1 setter sessions with decision fatigue, communication, and leadership demands, not just physical load.
training_considerations: train serve-receive play calls before the serve
include pressure scoring and bad-pass decision trees

physical_demands.name: Dual setter-attacker load
physical_demands.description: In a 6-2, setters typically set while back row and attack/block while front row. This creates a hybrid technical load: setting footwork and hand skill plus hitter/blocker jumping and landing.
physical_demands.backend_use: Build 6-2 athlete plans that do not treat setters as low-jump athletes.
training_considerations: monitor shoulder contacts from both setting and hitting
practice transition from defensive base into setting target

physical_demands.name: Libero low-posture reaction load
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
physical_demands.description: The libero avoids front-row attack and block jumps but carries high defensive exposure: serve receive, digging, emergency pursuit, repeated low posture, floor contacts, and rapid changes of direction.
physical_demands.backend_use: Avoid underestimating libero workload because regular jump count is lower.
training_considerations: train hip/ankle mobility and trunk control
include recovery from floor skills and shoulder-safe digging volume

physical_demands.name: Switching transition cost
source_refs: Why Should I Run a 6-3 or 6-6?
physical_demands.description: Specialized systems add switching paths after serve contact. More switching can improve role matchups but costs attention, movement time, and spacing safety.
physical_demands.backend_use: Add complexity score to rotation diagrams and drills; beginners should receive fewer switches.
training_considerations: introduce switching after players understand overlap
audit whether switching creates collisions or late attackers

injury_or_load_risks.name: Ankle sprain from net landing conflicts
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Net play creates repeated jump-land interactions; ankle sprains commonly occur when a player lands on another player's foot near the center line or net.
backend_implications: flag high block-jump drills for ankle-prevention warmups
pair front-row system work with landing-space education
include proprioceptive ankle work in volleyball S&C recommendations

injury_or_load_risks.name: Patellar tendinopathy from jump volume
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated attacking, blocking, and jump-serving load the knee extensor mechanism. Indoor players with high jump volumes and hard surfaces need managed volume and landing mechanics.
backend_implications: track planned jumps by position and system
avoid high-volume jump approach blocks on consecutive days
progress plyometrics only when landing control is acceptable

injury_or_load_risks.name: Shoulder overuse from attack, serve, and set volume
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Spiking, serving, and repeated overhead setting can overload the shoulder girdle, especially when technical fatigue changes mechanics.
backend_implications: separate overhead contact counts by role
include scapular strength and posterior shoulder mobility recommendations
watch 6-2 setter-attackers for combined setting and hitting volume

injury_or_load_risks.name: Low-back rotation and extension load
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated hitting, serving, emergency setting, and defensive extension can create cumulative low-back stress, especially when players compensate for other mobility or strength deficits.
backend_implications: include trunk strength and hip mobility in volleyball plans
avoid excessive maximal hitting when back discomfort is present
monitor back-row attack volume in advanced systems

injury_or_load_risks.name: Finger and thumb trauma from blocking and setting
source_refs: Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Blocking exposes the hands to high-speed attacks; setting and emergency contacts can stress fingers and thumbs.
backend_implications: progress blocking hand technique before high-velocity live attacks
add finger warm-up and taping education where appropriate
do not overload novice setters with long high-volume hand-setting blocks

injury_or_load_risks.name: Switching collision and spacing risk
source_refs: Why Should I Run a 6-3 or 6-6?
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Complex release and switching patterns can create crossing routes, late movements, and attention split between ball tracking and teammate traffic.
backend_implications: give each rotation a switching complexity score
teach route timing before live serve-receive pressure

source_refs: Why Should I Run a 6-3 or 6-6?
training_implications.recommendation: Teach rotation and row status before specialized systems. Use a simple 4-2, 6-6, or modified developmental system so players learn all skills, understand clockwise rotation, and reduce switching confusion.
avoid: complex setter penetration before players understand overlap
high jump volume in first system sessions
libero rules before players understand back-row status
assessment_items: Player can identify current position number and whether they are front row or back row.
Player can rotate clockwise correctly after side-out.
Player can name the two teammates they must stay relative to in serve receive.
Team can run a simple receive pattern without crossing routes or overlap faults.

training_implications.recommendation: Progress from simple 4-2 into 6-2 or 5-1 when the setter can reach target from back-row rotations and passers can preserve legal overlap while creating usable lanes.

system_choices.use_when: two setters can also attack and the team benefits from three front-row attackers
system_choices.watch_for: two setter tempos, substitution-budget constraints, and confusion over which setter takes second contact

system_choices.use_when: one setter is clearly the best offensive organizer and can handle all six rotations
system_choices.watch_for: front-row setter rotations with only two other front-row attackers and possible blocking mismatch at right front

assessment_items: Setter reaches target legally from each back-row rotation without early overlap release.
Back-row players avoid illegal above-net attacks from the front zone.
Libero replacements occur through the correct zone and do not consume regular substitutions.
Team can explain USAV vs FIVB substitution differences when rule set changes.

source_refs: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition
Principles of Prevention and Treatment of Common Volleyball Injuries
training_implications.recommendation: Train rotation-by-rotation side-out and transition plans. Use legal overlap compression, specialized release routes, scouting-based serve targets, and substitution/libero tactics while monitoring role-specific jump and overhead load.
assessment_items: Team has a planned first-ball side-out option for all six rotations.
Setter and hitters know legal back-row attack options by rotation.
Coaches can identify which rotations create two-attacker vs three-attacker front-row pressure.
Training plan balances system work with ankle, knee, shoulder, and low-back risk controls.

training_implications.recommendation: Store the active rule set explicitly. FIVB and USAV indoor rules are close enough for shared coaching models but different enough that substitution, libero serving, and designation rules should be variant-driven.
backend_requirements: Every match or training scenario should include ruleset_id.
Substitution recommendations must read ruleset_id before suggesting 6-2 or double-sub patterns.
Libero service availability must be false for FIVB and true only in the USAV one-rotation variant.
Rule update checks should reference official FIVB and USAV pages before production deployment.

records.description: Rule model for six-player rotation, receiving-team overlap, serving-team position freedom, side-out rotation, positional faults, and rotational faults.
Legal action matrix for front-row players, back-row players, and liberos.
Variant-aware libero model for replacement eligibility, attack restrictions, serving permission, and replacement sequencing.
Screening model for serving-team visibility and hand-height restrictions.

source_ref_titles: Rules of the Game Volleyball Casebook 2025 Edition

records.description: Reusable rotation state machine for line-up order, side-out rotation, front/back status, and server tracking.
Geometry validator for legal receiving-team serve-receive formations.
Beginner-friendly two-setter system with low switching and stable front-row setting.
Two setter-attacker system where the back-row setter runs offense and the front-row setter attacks.
Single-setter system prioritizing offensive continuity across all rotations.
Legal and tactical constraints for a non-libero front-row player.
Legal and tactical constraints for a non-libero back-row player.
Legal and tactical constraints for libero use.
Teaching sequence from basic six-player rotation into a low-switching 4-2.
Decision model for moving an intermediate team into 6-2 or 5-1.

choose_6_2_when: players can coordinate back-row setter release
choose_5_1_when: one setter clearly organizes offense best
team values one tempo and leader

records.description: Advanced rotation planning record for side-out, transition, matchup, and load management.
